Toyota's RAV4 PHEV Faces Software Issue That Can Disable Electric Drive
13 photos
Photo: Toyota
Currently the punchiest RAV4 that money can buy stateside, the plug-in hybrid makes up to 324 horsepower as long as the electric side of the powertrain operates without hiccups. The problem behind the latest Toyota Motor North America recall, however, starts with a controller that can take away electric propulsion due to iffy software.
When the motor-generator unit's control module fails to initialize correctly, the software may go kaput at higher speeds, leading to restricted front-drive operation. The worst-case scenario is a complete shutdown of the plug-in hybrid system. Approximately 30,978 vehicles are being recalled in the US market.
The initialization problem described by TMNA in the recall documentation occurs under certain startup conditions. Toyota further highlights that its consequences emerge when the compact-sized crossover reaches a speed that requires a compromised control mode. Warning lights instantly illuminate when the system shuts down or falls back to front-wheel drive in limp mode.
Neither outcome sounds particularly welcome, especially in a sport utility vehicle that promises up to 54 miles (87 kilometers) of all-electric range. In optimal conditions, both the internal combustion and electric sides of the powertrain come together to hit 60 miles per hour (97 kilometers per hour) in 5.4 seconds. The plug-in hybrid system relies on coordinated control of its electronics, and the recalled software can interfere with that coordination.
Per the NHTSA filing, G92A0-42460 is the part number of the motor generator's electronic control unit and inverter assembly. Supplied by Denso, this entire assembly is produced by a Japanese corporation that is partly owned by Toyota. Today, the Toyota Motor Corporation holds a 20 percent direct stake in Denso. Taking into account the entire group, Toyota owns just over 31 percent.
Photo: Toyota The largest automaker of them all by yearly sales learned about this condition after receiving a report from the Japanese market back in the summer. Warning lights had appeared during driving, and the vehicle could then operate only in FWD mode with its speed heavily restricted. The subsequent dealer inspection pointed to a communication malfunction as the rear motor generator swiches from its lower-speed control mode to high-speed control mode.
Bench tests provided the next clue, with Toyota determining that certain startup conditions prevent the rear motor-generator unit from completing initialization. When the higher-speed mode is requested, the system enters its programmed fail-safe state, increasing the risk of a crash.
Toyota then looked beyond the rear motor, for the front motor uses the same control program. By October 2026, the company had all the info required to call for a field service action. Produced in Japan, the US-market RAV4 PHEV recall population comprises 2026 models assembled between July 22, 2025, and August 19, 2026.
Through September 30, 2026, Toyota Motor North America received 58 warranty claims and 38 field technical reports from the US market. Considering that only software is to blame for this whole thing, dealers will gladly update the subject ECU software free of charge.
Customer notification letters should be mailed starting November 22, with the planned mailing period extending through December 6, 2026. Customers can check if their vehicles are potentially affected by running the VIN on the automaker's website or by using the NHTSA's lookup tool.
